The article is definitely sensationalist, sure. However, I have to point out here that anecdotal testimony isn't evidence, as much as we wish it were sometimes. If the claim that "A woman was forced to go into work the day after suffering a miscarriage" can actually be verified, for example, the assertion that Amazon isn't a good place to work could possibly be true - I don't really see another reason why a company wide refutation would need to be distributed from the desk of the CEO (IE It's strange that he would take his time to address this particular issue if everyone that works there is happy). On the other hand, the refutation you're pointing to here is entirely based upon "A guy who works there says he's never witnessed or experienced what's being claimed". This doesn't mean that it for sure doesn't happen. It means that it could be that A) He's correct, it doesn't actually exist, B) He's Never experienced or witnessed it but it does happen (He's ignorant of it) C) He does see it but marginalizes/justifies it, D) He willfully lied about it. I'm not sure if I've covered every option there, but it's enough to paint a picture of why anecdotal evidence is a little shaky - Someone can produce phone records of being ordered to go into work and their miscarriage, as the easy example, but it's difficult to prove the anecdotal "Everything is fine" is representative of the entire picture. This is also true of what @OjosAzules pointed out, unless the people venting on social media can produce evidence of some sort, it's difficult to say whether they're at all relevant either.
